# Ten Thousand Years of Population {#sec-history}

```{r}
#| label: setup-ch1
#| include: false
col_b <- "#1b9e3a"; col_d <- "#d62728"

## World population (millions); the file used in Lab 1
world <- read.table("data/world_population_data_2025.txt", header = TRUE,
                    comment.char = "#")

## Sweden (Human Mortality Database)
swe <- read.table("data/SWE_pop_birth_death.txt", header = TRUE)
swe$year <- as.numeric(rownames(swe))
swe$cbr <- 1000 * swe$B / swe$N
swe$cdr <- 1000 * swe$D / swe$N

## Growth rate from TFR and survival (lecture approximation):
## R ~ log(TFR * 0.4886 * survival to age 30) / 30
R_approx <- function(tfr, surv30) log(tfr * 0.4886 * surv30) / 30
```

**In this chapter.** What economic demography is about; how to measure
population growth; the long history of human numbers, from near-zero growth to
the explosion of the last two centuries; and the *demographic transition*.

**Readings this chapter draws on.** Livi-Bacci (2017), *A Concise History of
World Population*, Chapter 1, pp. 1–27; Congressional Budget Office (2024), "Effects of the
Immigration Surge on the Federal Budget and the Economy" (optional).
:::

::: {.column-margin}
[Added · new]{.tag-new} Bridge text written for the chapter split.
:::

This chapter is about the facts: how many people there have been, how fast their
numbers have grown, and why growth sped up and is now slowing. The next chapter,
@sec-optimum, uses the same course week's material to ask a normative question:
what size of population is *best*, and for whom?

## What is economic demography?

Economic demography asks two kinds of questions. The first half of this course
is about the **consequences** of population: how the number of people, and how
fast that number changes, affects human welfare. The second half is about the
**causes** of population change: the economic forces behind births, deaths,
migration, marriage, and divorce.

Two news stories show what this looks like.

### Example 1: China's "looming crisis"

In January 2019, the *New York Times* ran the headline "China's Looming Crisis:
A Shrinking Population." Four years later it reported that "China's Population
Falls, Heralding a Demographic Crisis": deaths had outnumbered births for the
first time in six decades.

If you grew up hearing that the world's problem was *too many* people, this
should raise some questions:

1. What's wrong with a shrinking population?
2. What is the best population size? Best for whom?
3. Why did population grow so much after 1950?
4. What limited growth in earlier centuries?
5. What will population change do to the environment?
6. And to inequality?

These questions run through the whole course. Note also that China's falling
fertility is not just a story about the one-child policy. Population growth was
slowing long before that policy, and has kept slowing since it ended. We return
to China in @sec-china.

### Example 2: The immigration surge

In July 2024, the Congressional Budget Office (CBO), the nonpartisan agency that
scores the federal budget for Congress, published an analysis of the recent
surge in immigration to the United States.

::: {.column-margin}
[Added · from readings]{.tag-reading} Figures in this subsection are from the
CBO report (2024), Summary and pp. 6, 19–21. The slides show CBO's Figures 1–2
and Table 2.
:::

CBO compared two scenarios. In its baseline, net immigration of the category it
calls "other foreign nationals" averages 1.7 million a year from 2021 to 2026.
In a counterfactual, it stays at the pre-2020 trend of 200,000 a year. The
difference, the "surge," is 8.7 million people. Counting their U.S.-born
children, the U.S. population in 2034 is about 10 million people, or nearly 3
percent, larger with the surge than without it.

CBO's headline findings:

- **The federal budget.** The surge *lowers* federal deficits by $0.9 trillion
  over 2024–2034. Immigrants in the surge pay $788 billion in income and payroll
  taxes. Benefits to them and their children add $177 billion to mandatory
  spending. The broader effects on the economy add more revenue than spending.
- **The economy.** Nominal GDP is $8.9 trillion higher over the decade. Most of
  that, $7.8 trillion, comes simply from having more people.

Should we conclude that the surge is "good for the economy"? Economic demography
teaches us to ask *for whom*, and *measured how*. A few things to notice:

::: {.column-margin}
[Added · new]{.tag-new} The per-capita comparison is my calculation from CBO's
numbers (real GDP +2.9% vs. population "nearly 3 percent" in 2034). It answers
one of the discussion questions in your course calendar.
:::

- **Totals versus per capita.** In 2034, real GDP is 2.9 percent higher because
  of the surge, and the population is nearly 3 percent larger. So GDP *per
  person* is roughly unchanged. A bigger economy is not the same as a richer
  population. Notice that CBO reports almost everything in totals.
- **Short run versus long run.** Through 2026, wage growth slows for workers with
  12 or fewer years of education, because there are more workers with similar
  skills. Later, wage growth speeds up slightly for all groups, as overall
  productivity rises.
- **Productivity can go both ways.** At first, the surge *lowers* average
  productivity, because the new arrivals have, on average, less education and work
  experience. Over time, the 3 percent of surge adults who work in science and
  engineering are expected to raise productivity through innovation, with the
  biggest effect 5 to 15 years after arrival. By 2034, CBO estimates, the two
  effects roughly cancel out.
- **Federal versus local.** CBO's estimates cover the federal budget only. It
  notes that research generally finds immigration raises state and local costs,
  especially for schools, more than state and local revenues.

The point is not that CBO is wrong. The report is careful and full of caveats.
The point is that "Is immigration good for the economy?" breaks into many
questions. There are perspectives to weigh: short term or long term, federal or
local government, the whole economy or per capita, capital or labor, rich or
poor, skilled or unskilled, producer or consumer. We take up immigration
directly at the end of the course.

## Measuring population growth

### Absolute or proportional change?

@tbl-world-pop shows estimates of world population over the last 10,000 years.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-world-pop
#| tbl-cap: "World population. Source: lecture slides (estimates from Weeks)."
#| echo: false
wp <- data.frame(year = c(-8000, 1, 500, 1000, 1500, 1750, 2000, 2015),
                 N = c(4, 211, 200, 290, 473, 764, 6080, 7218))
k <- nrow(wp)
abs_change <- c(diff(wp$N) / diff(wp$year), NA)            # millions per year
pct <- c(100 * diff(log(wp$N)) / diff(wp$year), NA)
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Year = wp$year,
  `Population (millions)` = format(wp$N, big.mark = ","),
  `Change (thousands per year)` = ifelse(is.na(abs_change), "",
                         format(round(1000 * abs_change), big.mark = ",")),
  `Growth rate (% per year)` = ifelse(is.na(pct), "", sprintf("%.2f", pct)),
  check.names = FALSE), align = "rrrr")
```

There are two ways to describe change. We could count the **absolute** change,
in persons per year. Or we could measure the **proportional** change, in
percent per year. Demographers usually prefer proportional change, for several
reasons:

- It is more constant over time.
- It connects naturally to individual behavior. Each person's chance of having a
  child or dying produces a growth *rate*, not a fixed number of new people.
- The underlying process is multiplicative. (The Bible says "be fruitful and
  multiply," not "be fruitful and add.")
- It connects to the other models we'll use, such as the Solow growth model.

But absolute change sometimes matters more. For the environment, for example,
what counts may be the total number of people burning fuel, not the rate at which
that number grows.

### The exponential model

The standard model of proportional growth is **exponential growth**:

$$
N(t) = N(0)\, e^{Rt},
$$

where $N(t)$ is the population at time $t$ and $R$ is the annual growth rate.
Taking natural logarithms of both sides and rearranging gives a formula for the
growth rate between any two dates:

$$
R = \frac{\log N(t) - \log N(0)}{t}.
$$

(Throughout this book, "log" means the natural logarithm, which is what R's
`log()` function computes.) This formula has a simple picture: $R$ is the
**slope** of the graph of log population against time, its "rise over run." For
example, world population grew from 6,080 million in 2000 to 7,218 million in 2015,
so

$$
R = \frac{\log(7218) - \log(6080)}{15} = `r round((log(7218) - log(6080)) / 15, 4)`,
$$

about `r round(100 * (log(7218) - log(6080)) / 15, 1)` percent per year.

::: {.column-margin}
[Added · new]{.tag-new} The "rule of 70" is not in your slides.
:::

A handy rule of thumb: a population growing at $R$ percent per year doubles in
about $70/R$ years. At 1 percent per year, it doubles in about 70 years. At 0.1
percent, it takes about 700 years.

### Seeing growth

@fig-world shows world population on the original scale and on a log scale,
using the data from Lab 1.

```{r}
#| label: fig-world
#| fig-cap: "World population, 8000 BCE to 2024, on the original scale (left) and a log scale (right). Data: Lab 1 file (Wikipedia; 2024 from the UN)."
#| fig-height: 3.8
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4.2, 2, 1))
plot(world$year, world$pop / 1000, type = "o", pch = 19, cex = 0.45, xaxt = "n",
     xlab = "Year", ylab = "Population (billions)", main = "Original scale",
     font.main = 1)
axis(1, at = seq(-8000, 2000, 2000))
plot(world$year, log(world$pop), type = "o", pch = 19, cex = 0.45, xaxt = "n",
     xlab = "Year", ylab = "log of population (millions)", main = "Log scale",
     font.main = 1)
axis(1, at = seq(-8000, 2000, 2000))
par(op)
```

On the original scale, nothing happens for ten thousand years and then
population explodes. The log scale shows proportional change, and it tells a
subtler story. For eight thousand years before the Common Era, log population
rose by about 4, a slope of about 4/8000 = 0.0005: growth of about 0.05 percent
per year. Since then, the slope has steepened again and again. Even the
*proportional* rate of growth has accelerated.

::: {.column-margin}
[Added · from readings]{.tag-reading} Livi-Bacci 2017, pp. 6–7 and Table 1.1.
:::

Livi-Bacci makes the same point with slightly different estimates. If world
population was 252 million at the start of the Common Era and 771 million in 1750,
average growth was only 0.06 percent per year. If the death rate averaged 40 per
thousand, then the birth rate must have averaged about 40.6: births exceeded
deaths by just 1.5 percent. For most of human history, he writes, "fertility and
mortality must have remained in virtual equilibrium." Since the 1960s, by
contrast, births have exceeded deaths by 200 percent.

@fig-world-growth plots the growth rate in each interval.

```{r}
#| label: fig-world-growth
#| fig-cap: "Average annual growth rate of world population in each interval between the dates in the Lab 1 data, plotted at the end of each interval. Left: 8000 BCE to 2024. Right: since 1900."
#| fig-height: 3.6
R_world <- 100 * diff(log(world$pop)) / diff(world$year)
end_year <- world$year[-1]
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4.2, 2, 1))
plot(end_year, R_world, type = "s", lwd = 2,
     xlab = "Year", ylab = "Growth rate (% per year)", main = "All periods",
     font.main = 1)
s <- end_year >= 1900
plot(end_year[s], R_world[s], type = "o", pch = 19, cex = 0.7, lwd = 2,
     xlab = "Year", ylab = "Growth rate (% per year)", main = "Since 1900",
     font.main = 1)
par(op)
```

The history of human population thus has three phases:

1. For most of human history, near-zero population growth.
2. Then a period of *accelerating* growth.
3. Most recently, *slowing* growth. The future of humanity may depend on how fast
   this slowing proceeds.

Explaining each phase is one of the goals of this course. Near-zero growth is
the subject of @sec-malthus. Accelerating and then slowing growth
is the subject of the demographic transition, below.

::: {.callout-important}

One more striking number from Livi-Bacci. Making "courageous" assumptions,
demographers estimate that about 82 billion people had been born by the year 2000.
The 6 billion alive in 2000 were thus about 7 percent of all the humans who have
ever lived.

## Generations, reproduction, and survival

### Paying the "demographic debt"

Population growth is ultimately a matter of generations. Does each generation of
parents raise enough children to replace itself?

::: {.column-margin}
[Added · from readings]{.tag-reading} The Bichi family and French Canadian
examples are from Livi-Bacci 2017, pp. 7–9.
:::

Livi-Bacci illustrates this with the descendants of Jacopo Bichi, a sharecropper
near Florence who married Domenica Del Buono in 1667. Over three generations, five
married couples of the family, ten spouses in all, raised nine children who in turn
married. Ten breeders brought nine offspring to reproduction: a 10 percent decline
per generation that, if repeated for long enough, would lead to the family's
extinction. Other families did better. The pioneers of French Canada, who settled
the St. Lawrence Valley in the seventeenth century, raised an average of 4.2
married children per couple. That is a doubling in a single generation. Two
pioneers, Jean Guyon and Mathurine Robin, had 2,150 descendants by 1730.

A population grows, shrinks, or stays the same depending on whether, on average,
each generation more than replaces, fails to replace, or exactly replaces itself.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## Try this (from class)
In lecture we simulate generational growth with the class itself. Each row is a
generation. Each person computes the "per parent" growth implied by their own
family (number of children in their parents' family, divided by two), and the
first row multiplies these together, row by row. Afterward, ask yourself: Is this
a good estimate of the growth rate of your parents' generation? What might be
wrong with it?
:::

### Two measures: fertility and survival

::: {.column-margin}
[Added · from readings]{.tag-reading} The components of fertility in this
subsection are from Livi-Bacci 2017, pp. 9–12.
:::

Two summary measures capture reproduction and survival:

- The **total fertility rate (TFR)** is the average number of children a woman
  would have over her reproductive life at current birth rates, in the absence of
  mortality. It is the most common summary measure of fertility. Before the
  demographic transition it exceeded 6. In the United States it has recently fallen
  to about 1.6, and in South Korea in 2023 it was 0.72.
- **Life expectancy at birth**, $e_0$, is the average number of years a newborn
  would live at current death rates.

What limits fertility in a society without birth control? Livi-Bacci breaks it
into two parts. The first is the **interval between births**, which is made up of
a period of infertility after each birth (longer when mothers breastfeed longer),
the waiting time to conceive, nine months of pregnancy, and time lost to
miscarriage. Together these give intervals of 1.5 to 3.5 years, usually 2 to 3.
The second is the **span of the reproductive period actually used**. That runs
from marriage, which may be as early as 15 or later than 25, to the end of
fecundity, with mothers' average age at last birth around 38 to 41. Combining the
extremes gives between 4.3 and 16.7 children per woman. In practice, averages below
5 or above 8 are rare. The two biggest levers are the **age at marriage** and the
**length of breastfeeding**. Hold onto the first: it is Malthus's preventive check.

Survival matters too, because a woman who dies young cannot have her children.
Livi-Bacci shows that when life expectancy at birth is 20 years, only about 29
percent of a generation's potential reproductive life is actually lived. At an
$e_0$ of 50 it is 71 percent, and at 83 it is 98 percent. If women would have 6
children each in the absence of mortality, high mortality cuts that to about 1.8
children per woman born.

### From TFR to growth rate

To turn the TFR into a growth rate, we need three adjustments:

- **Sex.** Only daughters go on to have children. About 48.86 percent of births are
  girls.
- **Mortality.** Only daughters who survive to childbearing age have children.
  Survival to about age 30 is a good summary.
- **Generation length.** Growth per generation must be converted to growth per
  year. A generation is about 30 years.

A good approximation is

$$
R \approx \frac{\log\left[\text{TFR} \times 0.4886 \times \text{survival to age 30}\right]}{30}.
$$

For example, with a TFR of 4 and survival to age 30 of 0.7, each woman is replaced
by 4 × 0.4886 × 0.7 = 1.37 surviving daughters, and
$R \approx \log(1.37)/30 \approx 0.01$, or 1 percent per year.

### The space of growth

::: {.column-margin}
[Added · new]{.tag-new} The figure is my construction, after your slide 02-31 and
Livi-Bacci's Figure 1.8. I approximate survival to 30 from $e_0$ with a smooth curve through
Livi-Bacci's three values (29%, 71%, 98%), plus endpoints I chose at $e_0$ = 15 and 95, and use your growth formula. The
discussion of age structure in the last paragraph is mine.
:::

Every combination of TFR and life expectancy implies a growth rate. @fig-isogrowth
draws curves of equal growth, "isogrowth" curves, and traces the path of world
population from 1700 to 2100 using estimates and projections from Ronald Lee
(@tbl-lee-world).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-lee-world
#| tbl-cap: "Global population trends over the transition, 1700–2100. Source: Lee, as shown in lecture."
#| echo: false
lee <- data.frame(year = c(1700, 1800, 1900, 1950, 2000, 2050, 2100),
                  e0 = c(27, 27, 30, 47, 65, 74, 81),
                  tfr = c(6.0, 6.0, 5.2, 5.0, 2.7, 2.0, 2.0),
                  pop = c(0.68, 0.98, 1.65, 2.52, 6.07, 8.92, 9.46),
                  R = c(0.50, 0.51, 0.56, 1.80, 1.22, 0.33, 0.04))
knitr::kable(setNames(lee, c("Year", "Life expectancy (years)", "TFR",
                             "Population (billions)", "Growth rate (% per year)")))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-isogrowth
#| fig-cap: "Isogrowth curves: combinations of life expectancy and TFR that imply the same long-run growth rate (labels are annual rates). Red: the world, 1700–2100 (Lee). Survival to age 30 is approximated from life expectancy using Livi-Bacci's figures."
#| fig-height: 5
surv_of_e0 <- splinefun(c(15, 20.7, 50.8, 83, 95), c(0.20, 0.292, 0.708, 0.982, 0.995),
                        method = "monoH.FC")
e0_grid <- seq(20, 90, 0.5); tfr_grid <- seq(1, 8, 0.05)
Rmat <- outer(e0_grid, tfr_grid, function(e, f) R_approx(f, surv_of_e0(e)))
op <- par(mar = c(4, 4.2, 1, 1))
contour(e0_grid, tfr_grid, Rmat, levels = seq(-0.02, 0.04, 0.01),
        col = "grey55", labcex = 0.8, drawlabels = TRUE,
        xlab = "Life expectancy at birth (years)",
        ylab = "Total fertility rate (children per woman)")
contour(e0_grid, tfr_grid, Rmat, levels = 0, lwd = 2.5, col = "grey30",
        add = TRUE, drawlabels = FALSE)
lines(lee$e0, lee$tfr, col = col_d, lwd = 2, type = "o", pch = 19, cex = 0.7)
text(lee$e0, lee$tfr, lee$year, col = col_d, cex = 0.8,
     pos = c(2, 4, 3, 3, 4, 1, 1))
par(op)
```

The thick curve is zero growth. Before 1900, the world sat in a narrow band just
above it, with low life expectancy and high fertility. Livi-Bacci notes that
pre-modern populations nearly all lived in the band between 0 and 1 percent growth,
though they got there in different ways. Denmark at the end of the eighteenth
century combined a life expectancy of about 40 with just over four children per
woman. India a century later combined a life expectancy of about 25 with just under
seven. During the twentieth century, life expectancy rose first, carrying the world
far above the zero line, before fertility fell and brought it back down.

One caution. The curves show the *long-run* growth rate that a combination of
fertility and mortality would eventually produce. Actual growth in a given year
also depends on the population's age structure. In 2000, the world's TFR of 2.7
implies long-run growth of only a few tenths of a percent per year. Actual growth
was 1.2 percent, because the world's population was young, with many people of
childbearing age. That momentum takes decades to work itself out.

### Environmental constraints

::: {.column-margin}
[Added · from readings]{.tag-reading} This subsection summarizes Livi-Bacci
2017, pp. 2–5 and 19–24. Your slides don't cover it.
:::

Why did population grow so slowly for so long? Livi-Bacci begins with biology.
Species follow different reproductive "strategies." *r-strategists* (insects,
fish, small mammals) have many offspring and invest little in each, and their
numbers swing violently. *K-strategists* (large mammals, including humans) have few
offspring, invest heavily in each, and stay in more stable balance with their
environment. Humans are an extreme K-strategy species.

Within that biology, the environment sets limits. Hunter-gatherers lived at
densities of about 0.1 to 1 person per square kilometer, limited by the plants and
animals available within a day's walk. Agriculture raised the limit enormously. By
the mid-eighteenth century, the major European countries had 40 to 60 people per
square kilometer, about 100 times the density of hunter-gatherers. But farming still
depended on plants and animals for energy, and so ultimately on land. Hunter-gatherers
used about 5,000 calories of energy per person per day, and farming societies never
more than about 12,000 to 26,000. The industrial revolution broke the link between
energy and land: early industrial societies used about 70,000 calories per person
per day, and some today use more than 200,000.

So each great technological era, hunting and gathering, agriculture, and
industry, raised the ceiling on human numbers. Population then grew toward the new
ceiling and slowed as it approached it. This is the idea, common to animal biology
and to Malthus, that growth slows as density rises. We develop it in the next
chapter.

## The demographic transition

### Crude rates

The simplest measures of births and deaths are the **crude birth rate**, annual
births divided by population, written $b$, and the **crude death rate**, annual
deaths divided by population, written $d$. ("Crude" because the denominator is
everyone, men and women, young and old.) Without migration, the growth rate is just

$$
R = b - d.
$$

Typical values: about 40 deaths per thousand per year in ancient Rome, about 10 in
modern Japan, and about 8 in the modern United States. (Is it really more dangerous
to be born in Japan than in the United States? Think about age structure.)

### A puzzle, seen from the 1970s

Today the demographic transition can seem obvious: birth and death rates used to be
high, and now both are low. But put yourself in the position of an observer in the
1970s. World population growth had been accelerating for centuries. Energy prices
were skyrocketing, environmental worries were rising, and economic growth was
slowing. If you saw the sequence 1, 1, 1, 1, 2, 3, what number would you predict
next?

Predicting the future requires understanding the *system* that produces births and
deaths. Perhaps both depend on income: $b(y)$ and $d(y)$. Perhaps both depend on
population size: $b(N)$ and $d(N)$. Perhaps mortality changes for its own reasons,
and fertility responds to mortality: $b(d)$. The next several chapters explore
these possibilities.

### An idealized picture

@fig-dt-ideal shows the demographic transition in its idealized form.

```{r}
#| label: fig-dt-ideal
#| fig-cap: "An idealized demographic transition. Left: crude birth and death rates. Right: the growth rate, R = b − d. High growth is just a phase."
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| echo: false
t <- seq(0, 100, 0.5)
set.seed(2)
cdr <- 10 + 28 / (1 + exp((t - 35) / 4)) + ifelse(t < 25, 2.5 * sin(t / 1.6), 0)
cbr <- 10 + 30 / (1 + exp((t - 60) / 5))
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(3, 4, 2, 1), mgp = c(2, 0.5, 0))
plot(t, cbr, type = "l", lwd = 2.5, col = col_b, ylim = c(0, 45),
     xaxt = "n", yaxt = "n", xlab = "Time", ylab = "Crude rates",
     main = "Birth and death rates", font.main = 1)
lines(t, cdr, lwd = 2.5, col = col_d)
text(70, 33, "Birth rate", col = col_b)
text(18, 15, "Death rate", col = col_d)
arrows(48, cdr[t == 48] + 0.5, 48, cbr[t == 48] - 0.5, code = 3,
       length = 0.06, col = "grey30")
text(48, (cdr[t == 48] + cbr[t == 48]) / 2, "R", pos = 4)
plot(t, cbr - cdr, type = "l", lwd = 2.5, xaxt = "n", yaxt = "n",
     xlab = "Time", ylab = "Growth rate (R)", main = "Growth rate",
     font.main = 1)
abline(h = 0, lty = 3)
par(op)
```

- **Before the transition:** high fertility and high mortality. Mortality
  fluctuates with random shocks such as epidemics and harvest failures.
- **During the transition:** mortality falls first, and the decline in fertility
  lags behind. The gap between them produces *transitional growth*.
- **After the transition:** fertility finally falls too. Now the fluctuations in
  growth come from fertility, and fertility may fall below replacement.

Some typical numbers. Before the transition, the TFR exceeds 6, and life
expectancy is about 40 to 50 years or less. In Korea in 1950, the crude birth rate
was 37 per thousand and the death rate 32, for growth of half a percent. During the
transition, growth rates reached 1 to 2 percent in historical Europe and 3 to 4
percent in Africa. In Iraq in 1985, the birth rate was 42 per thousand and the
death rate 8, for growth of 3.4 percent. After the transition, the TFR is around 2
(or 2.5, or 1.5), life expectancy is 70 or 80, and growth is near zero. Belgium in
1984 had a birth rate of 12 per thousand and a death rate of 11.

### Sweden

@fig-swe-dt shows the transition in Sweden, using the Human Mortality Database
data we use in Lab 2. (In lecture we compare Sweden with Mexico, where the
transition came later and was much faster.)

```{r}
#| label: fig-swe-dt
#| fig-cap: "The demographic transition in Sweden: crude birth and death rates, 1751–2014. The shaded area between the curves from 1800 to 1900 is the sum of annual growth rates over the century. Source: Human Mortality Database."
#| fig-height: 4
op <- par(mar = c(4, 4.2, 1, 1))
plot(swe$year, swe$cbr, type = "n", ylim = c(0, 55),
     xlab = "Year", ylab = "Per 1,000 population")
s <- swe$year %in% 1800:1900
polygon(c(swe$year[s], rev(swe$year[s])), c(swe$cbr[s], rev(swe$cdr[s])),
        col = adjustcolor(col_b, 0.18), border = NA)
lines(swe$year, swe$cbr, col = col_b, lwd = 1.5)
lines(swe$year, swe$cdr, col = col_d, lwd = 1.5)
legend("topright", c("Crude birth rate", "Crude death rate"),
       col = c(col_b, col_d), lwd = 2, bty = "n")
par(op)
area <- sum((swe$B[swe$year %in% 1800:1899] - swe$D[swe$year %in% 1800:1899]) /
            swe$N[swe$year %in% 1800:1899])
ratio <- swe$N[swe$year == 1900] / swe$N[swe$year == 1800]
```

Sweden's death rate began a long, slow decline in the late eighteenth century. The
birth rate stayed high until the 1870s and then fell, reaching death-rate levels by
the 1930s. The gap between them, the shaded area, is transitional growth.

There is a neat way to use such a picture. Because growth rates add up on the log
scale, the total growth over a period is $e$ raised to the *sum* of the annual
growth rates, which is the area between the birth and death curves. For Sweden from
1800 to 1900, that area is about `r round(area, 2)`, which implies the population
should have multiplied by $e^{`r round(area, 2)`} \approx `r round(exp(area), 2)`$.

::: {.column-margin}
[Added · new]{.tag-new} The emigration explanation is my addition. The numbers
are computed from the HMD data. Note: slide 02-27 lists "Sweden 1900 2.3 million,
2000 5 million." The HMD has 2.35 million in 1800 and 5.10 million in 1900, so the
slide's years look like they should be 1800 and 1900.
:::

In fact, Sweden grew from `r round(swe$N[swe$year == 1800] / 1e6, 2)` million in
1800 to `r round(swe$N[swe$year == 1900] / 1e6, 2)` million in 1900, a factor of
only `r round(ratio, 2)`. Where did the missing growth go? Births minus deaths
leaves out **migration**, and nineteenth-century Sweden sent large numbers of
emigrants to the United States. The formula $R = b - d$ holds only for a closed
population.

### The world

Return to @tbl-lee-world. World life expectancy rose from 27 years in 1800 to 65 in
2000, and is projected to reach 81 by 2100. The TFR fell from 6 to 2.7 and is
projected to reach 2. Growth peaked at about 1.8 percent per year around 1950 and is
projected to approach zero by 2100. On @fig-isogrowth you can see the transitional
growth as the excursion above the zero-growth line, and you can see how growth
depends jointly on life expectancy and fertility.

The stylized facts we want to explain, then, are **stationarity → transitional
growth → stationarity (?)**. The next chapter asks a normative question:
what population size is *optimal*, and for whom? @sec-malthus then turns to Malthus,
his "trap," and why neither population nor the economy grew much for thousands of
years.

## Key ideas

- Economic demography studies the **consequences** of population for welfare and the
  **causes** of population change. Totals and per-capita measures can tell very
  different stories.
- Population growth is best measured **proportionally**. In the exponential model,
  the growth rate is the slope of log population:
  $R = [\log N(t) - \log N(0)]/t$.
- Human history has three phases: near-zero growth for millennia, accelerating growth,
  and recently slowing growth.
- Growth depends on **fertility** (TFR) and **survival**:
  $R \approx \log(\text{TFR} \times 0.4886 \times \text{survival to 30})/30$.
- In the **demographic transition**, mortality falls first and fertility follows,
  producing a temporary burst of growth.

2. **Absolute versus proportional.** World population grew by more people per year
   from 1750 to 2000 than in any earlier period, and it will likely continue adding
   tens of millions a year even as the growth *rate* falls. Give one question for
   which the absolute number matters more than the rate, and one for which the rate
   matters more.

   in 2034. What other number do you need to judge whether the average U.S. resident

## Further reading

- Livi-Bacci, Massimo. 2017. "The Space and Strategy of Demographic Growth." Chapter
  1 of *A Concise History of World Population*, 6th ed. Wiley. Pages 1–27.
  *A broad overview mixing biology, economics, and demography. It sets the stage for
  Malthusian constraints and the growth theories later in the course.*
- Congressional Budget Office. 2024. "Effects of the Immigration Surge on the Federal
  Budget and the Economy." July. *Optional. As you read: Which results would you want
  to see per capita? Why doesn't CBO present things that way? Why does the surge first
  lower and then raise productivity?*
